facts.fact_text: On 22 April 2000, the applicant organised a demonstration in Sultanahmet Square in Istanbul.
The demonstration organised by the applicant on 22 April 2000 took the form of a march followed by a statement to the press.
The demonstration organised by the applicant on 22 April 2000 was held to protest against plans for 'F-type' prisons.
At about 12 noon on 22 April 2000, a group of forty to fifty persons gathered in Sultanahmet Square brandishing placards and signs.
The group of forty to fifty persons gathered in Sultanahmet Square under the leadership of the applicant and Eren Keskin.
The police asked the group gathered in Sultanahmet Square to disperse and to end the gathering.
The police dispersed the group of demonstrators using a kind of tear gas known as 'pepper spray'.
The police arrested thirty-nine demonstrators, including the applicant.
The police took the thirty-nine arrested demonstrators, including the applicant, to a police station.
In her criminal complaint of 26 April 2000, the applicant alleged that she had been prevented from making the public statement scheduled for the end of the demonstration.
Article 34 of the Turkish Constitution provides that everyone has the right to hold unarmed and peaceful meetings and demonstration marches without prior permission.

Article 34 of the Turkish Constitution provides that the formalities, conditions, and procedures governing the exercise of the right to hold meetings and demonstration marches shall be prescribed by law.

At the material time, section 10 of Law no. 2911 on assemblies and marches required that, in order for a meeting to take place, the governor's office or authorities of the district in which the demonstration is planned must be informed during opening hours and at least seventy-two hours prior to the meeting.
Under section 10 of Law no. 2911 on assemblies and marches, the required notice must contain the signature of all the members of the organising board.
Section 22 of Law no. 2911 on assemblies and marches prohibits demonstrations and processions on public streets, in parks, places of worship, and buildings in which public services are based.

Under section 22 of Law no. 2911 on assemblies and marches, demonstrations organised in public squares must comply with security instructions and not disrupt individuals' movement or public transport.

Section 24 of Law no. 2911 on assemblies and marches provides that demonstrations and processions which do not comply with the provisions of that Act will be dispersed by force on the order of the governor's office and after the demonstrators have been warned.

The European Commission for Democracy through Law (the Venice Commission) adopted an opinion interpreting the OSCE/ODHIR guidelines on drafting laws on freedom of assembly with regard to the regulation of public meetings at its 64th plenary session held on 21-22 October 2005.
The Venice Commission's opinion set out its approach particularly with regard to advance notice of demonstrations in public places.

The Venice Commission stated in paragraph 29 of its opinion that establishing a regime of prior notification of peaceful assemblies does not necessarily extend to an infringement of the right to freedom of assembly, and that such regimes exist in several European countries.

The Venice Commission stated in paragraph 29 of its opinion that the need for advance notice generally arises in respect of certain meetings or assemblies — for instance, when a procession is planned to take place on the highway, or a static assembly is planned to take place on a public square — which require the police and other authorities to enable it to occur and not to use powers that they may validly have (for instance, of regulating traffic) to obstruct the event.

The Venice Commission emphasised in paragraph 30 of its opinion that the regime of prior notification must not in any circumstances indirectly restrict the right to hold peaceful meetings by, for instance, providing for too detailed and complicated requirements, or imposing too onerous procedural conditions.

Under Article I § 5 of the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction of 13 January 1993 (the CWC), each State Party undertakes not to use riot control agents as a method of warfare.

Tear gas and so-called 'pepper spray' are not considered chemical weapons under the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction of 13 January 1993 (the CWC), which contains an annex listing the names of prohibited chemical products.

Under Article II § 9(d) of the Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction of 13 January 1993 (the CWC), the use of tear gas and pepper spray is authorised for the purpose of law enforcement, including domestic riot control.

The Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction of 13 January 1993 (the CWC) does not state which State bodies may be involved in maintaining public order, leaving this as a matter for the sovereign power of the State concerned.

The Convention on the Prohibition of the Development, Production, Stockpiling and Use of Chemical Weapons and on their Destruction of 13 January 1993 (the CWC) entered into force with regard to Turkey on 11 June 1997.

It is recognised that the use of 'pepper spray' can produce effects such as respiratory problems, nausea, vomiting, irritation of the respiratory tract, irritation of the tear ducts and eyes, spasms, chest pain, dermatitis, or allergies.
It is recognised that in strong doses, 'pepper spray' may cause necrosis of tissue in the respiratory or digestive tract.
It is recognised that in strong doses, 'pepper spray' may cause pulmonary oedema.
It is recognised that in strong doses, 'pepper spray' may cause internal haemorrhaging, specifically haemorrhaging of the suprarenal gland.
On 26 April 2000, the applicant lodged a criminal complaint with the Beyoğlu prosecutor's office against the head of the Istanbul security police and the police officers concerned.
In her criminal complaint of 26 April 2000, the applicant alleged that she had been ill-treated through the use of pepper spray.
In her criminal complaint of 26 April 2000, the applicant alleged that she had been unlawfully arrested.
In her criminal complaint of 26 April 2000, the applicant alleged that she had been prevented from making the public statement scheduled for the end of the demonstration.

On 29 June 2000, the public prosecutor's office discontinued the proceedings against the head of the Istanbul security police and the police officers concerned on the ground that no offence had been committed.
On 25 July 2000, the applicant applied to the Beyoğlu Assize Court seeking to have the decision of 29 June 2000 to discontinue proceedings set aside.
On 25 September 2000, the Beyoğlu Assize Court upheld the decision that there was no case to answer.
